pr_title: kubelet, kube-proxy: unmark packets before masquerading them
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
As noted by @tommasopozzetti in #88986, we appear to be double-NAT-ing some packets due to oddness about how the packet mark works in the kernel. (Routing a packet through a VXLAN tunnel reuses the same kernel packet object and sends it through the network stack a second time. In particular, it does not reset the packet mark when this happens, so as a result if we call `KUBE-MARK-MASQ` on a packet and then later route that packet through a VXLAN tunnel, then `KUBE-POSTROUTING` will end up NAT-ing first the original packet, and then later the outer VXLAN-encapsulating packet.) The superfluous NAT-ing of the outer packet, combined with our use of `iptables -j MASQUERADE --random-fully`, results in us hitting a kernel packet checksum bug which then causes dropped packets and severe performance problems.

Although the kernel bug has been fixed, the fact that we are double-NAT-ing is still not great. #78948 mentions a few smaller issues, and apparently it might also cause performance problems by making the VXLAN packets look unrelated to each either due to their differing source ports, causing them to end up in different rx queues on the destination side (which I guess means successive packets might not all be processed by the same CPU or something?)

Additionally, fixing it here means it will be fixed even for people who can't easily upgrade to a fixed kernel.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #88986
Fixes #90854
(and various flannel/weave/calico/etc issues)

**Special notes for your reviewer**:
This changes `KUBE-POSTROUTING` from "if marked for masquerade then masquerade" to "if _not_ marked for masquerade then return to `POSTROUTING`, else unmark and then masquerade". This required some extra rewriting of the code though because it was previously doing `-set-xmark 0x4000/0x4000` to set the bit and `--mark 0x4000/0x4000` to match it, but there's no way to _clear_ the mark using the string `0x4000/0x4000` so I had to rewrite it in terms of `0x4000` instead.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:

```release-note
Fixes a problem with 63-second or 1-second connection delays with some VXLAN-based
network plugins which was first widely noticed in 1.16 (though some users saw it
earlier than that, possibly only with specific network plugins). If you were previously
using ethtool to disable checksum offload on your primary network interface, you should
now be able to stop doing that.
```

(EDIT: Further explanation of both the kube bug and the kernel bug and how they interact [in this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/92035#issuecomment-652395132))

/sig network
/priority important-soon

I think the reason it is not working is because the rule is not actually doing a XOR to cancel the marker but rather an OR (so the marker persists).

I think it is due to the behavior of `--set-xmark`

```
--set-xmark value[/mask]
Zeroes out the bits given by mask and XORs value into the packet mark ("nfmark"). If mask is omitted, 0xFFFFFFFF is assumed.
```

So I think doing `--set-xmark 0x4000/0x4000` actually does `nfmark = (nfmark AND NOT 0x4000) XOR 0x4000` which is equal to `nfmark = nfmark OR 0x4000`
I think doing `--set-xmark 0x4000/0` should do the trick as it should be `nfmark = (nfmark AND NOT 0) XOR 0x4000` which is equal to `nfmark = nfmark XOR 0x4000`

@danwinship 
Because the 63s delay is caused by the checksum (five times TCP retransmission, 1s + 2s + 4s+ 8s+ 16s + 32s = 63s),
so I have some quesitons:
1.  Is the incorrect checksum triggered by the double SNAT or with something else?
2. Does the --random-fully argument influence checksum?

Can you give some ideas, thanks.

So a packet gets masqueraded, then later encapsulated in a VXLAN packet. The source IP for the VXLAN packet is the node's IP, and the source port is something random. At some point, the UDP checksum gets computed for that packet. Then, because of the bug that was fixed here, we end up calling `-j MASQUERADE` on the VXLAN packet even though it doesn't need it.

Pre-1.16, we weren't using the `--random-fully` mode of `-j MASQUERADE`, so the kernel NAT code would try to preserve the packet's original source port when masquerading it. Since the source IP was already the node's IP (and thus didn't need to be changed as part of masquerading it), and the source port could be preserved, that means that the masquerading step didn't change the packet at all, so the checksum that was previously computed was still correct, and the packet gets sent off and everythign works.

But when we started using `--random-fully`, that meant that when the NAT code was called for the second time, it intentionally did not preserve the same source port when masquerading the VXLAN, so the port changed, and thus the checksum needed to be recomputed. But because of the kernel bug, the checksum _didn't_ get recomputed, and so the receiving node would reject the packet because it had a bad checksum.

Fixing the kernel checksum bug makes the problem go away even if the double-NAT bug is still there, because the packet will now get correctly rechecksummed after the second NAT. Fixing the double NAT bug fixes the problem even if the kernel checksum bug is still there, because the VXLAN packet now won't get masqueraded, so it doesn't need to be rechecksummed.

**What happened**:
From a computer (ghana) outside my dev cluster (tonga, spain) I can access a micro service via its NodePort (in the following the service just responds with the string "Im not well. Please restart me!")
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76258380-ce260200-6229-11ea-9fd5-a876d20415e9.png)


But when I try to access the service either via its ClusterIP, or via its EXTERNAL-IP, I see a delay in routing the request to a pod on "the other node". 

I intially thought this might be a problem with MetalLB, however I've now taken MetalLB out of the loop completely, and see this problem when accessing the service via the ClusterIP. 

**Cluster IP curl - (10.96.11.2)**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76563644-2f461380-647e-11ea-9881-344ce77d690f.png)

 **EXTERNAL-IP curl (192.168.1.241**)
Though the following picture is with the NodePort (30123), I've also tried the PORT(8080)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76258522-1e04c900-622a-11ea-9409-c3f88b0840c0.png)

**The pictures show**
From a node inside the cluster, I am able to curl to the service using either its ClusterIP:PORT or its EXTERNAL-IP:PORT, but when that curl request is routed to a pod in the cluster, _that is on the other node_, it takes **_63_** seconds for the request to arrive at the pod on that node

This delay (of 1 minute) is seen in the following picture.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76452938-4ca8ae00-63a8-11ea-8243-2c6140f79ea2.png)

In the following I am running tcpdump on the traffic to the PODS IP (10.244.2.5). 

As soon as I perform the curl I see several packets that flow to port (8080) "webcache" . Its not until 1 minute later that I see the message that triggers the request sent to the pod itself... then the pod responds.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76454343-df4a4c80-63aa-11ea-9cd7-3bc85c9c2e93.png)

It seems that the first series of SYN packets dont get through.

**Interesting Note**
Its interesting to see that the SYN packets that lead up to the successful request have increasing time delays (in seconds): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Then we see the SYN ACK from the kubia service.

It seems that the packet is being sent to the POD IP, however that packet is not routed to the container entrypoint.


I've also posted [this delay problem](https://discuss.kubernetes.io/t/bare-metal-k8s-load-balancer-service-routing-delay/10035) on the k8s forum.

**What you expected to happen**:
curl to EXTERNAL_IP:SERVICE_PORT (192.168.1.241:8080) 
or to 
curl to CLUSTER_IP:SERVICE_PORT (10.96.11.2:8080) 

should succeed, promptly (within just a few msec)

**Update**
Because I've learned a bit and isolated a bit (since first writing this issue), please go to my last comment, and "read up". 

The comments starting with the one that says "Hmmm.. What i find is that I'm able to curl the pod port 8080 sometimes when i run the curl on the master, but not when I run it from outside the cluster." are most informative.

I've captured my latest understanding in those comments. 

**In short, I'm seeing an unexpected 60 second delay in response to service queries that get Load Balanced to the other node. Further, I dont seem to be able to hit the EXTERNAL-IP from outside the cluster (those requests never seem to make it to the pod, though they do make it to the cluster nodes).**


**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
On a bare metal cluster, create and deploy a service such as the one below:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76312627-d291ff80-62a9-11ea-9066-00ad58830a34.png)

I deployed the micro service using a replicaset.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76314414-218d6400-62ad-11ea-98c1-1693af54ee4b.png)

Expose the service via a LoadBalancer.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76315322-da07d780-62ae-11ea-81c7-79a4899616a3.png)


The following service description illustrates the pod EndPoints for the 2 pod replicas
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76319620-de83be80-62b5-11ea-8b49-7f1cf98a5dc8.png)

In the following we see that kube-proxy has properly bound to the NodePort on my k8s nodes
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76316299-bcd40880-62b0-11ea-8fc5-82ff8cfee05e.png)


Install [MetalLB](https://metallb.universe.tf/concepts/layer2/).

I used 
`kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/metallb/v0.8.3/manifests/metallb.yaml`

with layer 2 configuration as depicted [here](https://metallb.universe.tf/configuration/).

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48793689/76315451-13404780-62af-11ea-995e-bec4a0a8499d.png)


On a box outside the cluster add a logical network and assign an IP on that network

On ghana (my test client box outside the cluster) I used the following (em1 is a physical interface that can connect to the k8s cluster):
`ifconfig em1:0 192.168.1.243 255.255.255.0`

I also tried 192.168.1.239 (outside the range owned by MetalLB - based on the configuration above)

The following would also work.
`ip addr add 192.168.1.243/24 dev em1 label em1:0`

Now its possible to use that logical network to curl 192.168.1.241 (the EXTERNAL-IP assigned by MetalLB) at port 30123 (the NodePort that kube-proxy binds to associated with the LoadBalancer service.

tcpdump on any of the k8s nodes can verify that the curl request arrives at port 30123 (the port kube-proxy has bound) on the k8s node. 

tcpdump can also be used to verify that kube-proxy does not respond (with SYN-ACK) to the SYN bit found with curls  "synchronize" request.

My ingress was passing requests to a `Service` that was using `ExternalName` (i.e. pointing to a DNS name like _some-service.some-namespace.svc.cluster.local_).

- DNS Requests from `NodeA - Nginx` -> `NodeB - CoreDNS` would time out, but
- DNS Requests from `NodeA - Nginx` -> `NodeA - CoreDNS` would succeed.

> ... If no port range is specified, then source ports  below  512 will be mapped to other ports below 512: those between 512 and 1023 inclusive will be mapped to ports below 1024, and other ports will be mapped to 1024  or  above.  **Where possible,  no  port alteration will occur.**

Emphasis added. But checking [the source](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v5.6/net/netfilter/nf_nat_core.c#L543), that last part is only true if you _don't_ pass `--random` or `--random-fully`:

```
	if (maniptype == NF_NAT_MANIP_SRC &&
	    !(range->flags & NF_NAT_RANGE_PROTO_RANDOM_ALL)) {
		/* try the original tuple first */
```

So with the old non-`--random-fully` code, most of the time, the NATted packet will have the same source port as the original packet, but if you _do_ use `--random-fully`, then it's guaranteed that the NAT code will have to change the source port in the packet, which means it will have to fix up its checksum after NATting it, which means it hits the checksum offload bug. BOOM.

OK, so this is good. It confirms that `--random-fully` isn't itself buggy, it's just that it causes us to reliably hit the other bug. Now to figure out what to do about this...

So... @kubernetes/sig-network-misc it seems that using `iptables --random-fully` definitely triggers the udp checksum / vxlan bug, just because of the nature of how it works, not because `--random-fully` is buggy. And there's no workaround other than not using `--random-fully` or avoiding the checksum bug. At the moment, there are probably more people being hurt by our use of `--random-fully` than are being helped by it, but over time that will change, as people get the kernel updates that fix the checksum bug.

So...

1. We could do nothing and just require affected users to either upgrade their kernels or disable checksum offload. (There is not yet a RHEL 7 kernel with the checksum bug fix and I'm not sure when there will be.)
2. Revert `--random-fully` entirely, at least for now, possibly breaking users who were depending on it (eg, #76699, ~though FTR it's not actually confirmed that `--random-fully` fixed things for them~)
3. Only use `--random-fully` when there are no VXLAN interfaces on the system (so non-VXLAN-using network plugins can get the benefits of `--random-fully`, while VXLAN-using plugins don't, but continue working with older kernels).
4. Only use `--random-fully` when the kernel is of a version known to have the checksum fix
5. Add a kube-proxy arg saying whether to use `--random-fully`.

We have also been wrestling with this bug. We use calico with VXLAN, but the issue is precisely the same and seems to be related mostly to the vxlan interface and not really to flannel/calico. I did some digging and I found the following info, hopefully it can be useful to figure out a solution:

As others have mentioned, the 1 second delay seems to derive from a retransmission of the SYN packet when setting up the TCP connection to a service clusterIP.

By inspecting the packets on the network and in the hosts, I found that the packet actually makes it to the other end of the VXLAN tunnel (the encapsulated packet is received by the destination host) but gets dropped by the receiving vxlan interface, most likely due to the UDP checksum issue.

The reason why this is only seen on certain configurations (for example when hitting a nodePort or when establishing the connection from within a host networked pod/a host node but not from within a non-host networked pod) is due to the source IP and the following iptables rules in the `nat` table (these are for a system with kube-proxy set in ipvs mode but similar rules are present for kube-proxy in iptables mode, they are just less aggregated):
```
-A KUBE-NODE-PORT -p tcp -m comment --comment "Kubernetes nodeport TCP port for masquerade purpose" -m set --match-set KUBE-NODE-PORT-TCP dst -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
-A KUBE-SERVICES ! -s <pod_ip_range> -m comment --comment "Kubernetes service cluster ip + port for masquerade purpose" -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j KUBE-MARK-MASQ
```

The `KUBE-MARK-MASQ` target marks the packet so that it will perform SNAT in the `POSTROUTING` table using the `--random-fully` flag.

What seems to be happening, is that when such rules are hit for a packet that will need to go through a VXLAN tunnel, the `0x4000` mark is attached to the packet and persists with it in the kernel even after the packet has been routed to the vxlan interface and incapsulated in the UDP packet from source host to destination host. This causes the `POSTROUTING` rules to actually perform a further SNAT operation on the UDP packet leaving the host.
Here is when things seem to line up to create the issue: because the packet actually already has as source IP the IP of the host, this SNAT should not be needed (and the source IP will not change if it is performed). The source port could be changed, but normally the same original port is tried first and, given that it will normally be available, it is not changed so the SNAT becomes a no-op. Because of `--random-fully`, however, the port is always changed, which causes this SNAT to actually only change the source port. This is however enough to require recalculation of the UDP checksum, which seems to hit the bug that will cause the packet to be discarded by the receiving vxlan interface.

A few changes which seem to have eliminated the 1 second delay:
1) Disabling offload on the vxlan interface, which seems to cause the UDP checksum to be recalculated correctly without hitting this bug
2) Adding an iptables rule at the top of the `OUTPUT` chain in the `nat` table to clear the `0x4000` mark for VXLAN UDP packets leaving the host. This seems to avoid the useless SNAT which changes the source port and forces a UDP checksum recalculation, and it seems to remove the 1 second delay. This is the solution we have adopted for now and it seems to be working correctly:
```
-A OUTPUT -p udp -m udp --dport 8472 -j MARK --set-xmark 0x0
```
3) Modify the iptables rules that set the `0x4000` mark on packets to avoid doing so not only for source IPs in the pod ip range but also from the host IP itself. I'm not sure if this can have further implications on other functionalities, but it seems reasonable that if the source IP is that of the host itself, there should be no reason to mark the packet for performing SNAT to begin with. This would allow treating host-networked pods the same way non-host-networked pods are treated. I have only quickly tested this solution by creating an ipset and using it in the rule for clusterIPs and it seems to have eliminated the delay, but I did not test it cluster-wide nor for nodePort (even though I assume it would be the same applied to the other iptables rule).
